claim: The Drosophila genome annotation contains 829 smORF genes, representing 4% of the total genes.
source: The annotation of the Drosophila genome contains double the proportion of predicted smORF-encoding genes than other metazoan genomes (some 829 smORF genes, or 4% of the total, Table 1) (FlyBase, Ensembl).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from FlyBase and Ensembl databases as cited in the text, and is corroborated by Table 1 which shows the numbers.

claim: Only 164 annotated smORFs have at least two out of three markers indicating translation or peptide function.
source: Only 164 annotated smORFs have at least two out of three markers indicating translation or peptide function: (1) molecular GO term indicating protein function (based on direct assays or presence of protein domains); (2) matches with peptides from proteomic experiments; and (3) conservation of the coding sequence beyond insects (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multiple data types (GO terms, proteomics, conservation) as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 665 putative smORFs have uncorroborated translation status.
source: The translation of the remaining 665 putative smORFs is thus not yet fully proven, and in most cases (494 smORFs) no evidence of translation is recorded.
evidence: The claim is derived from analysis of annotation data and evidence categories presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq isolates mRNAs bound by multiple ribosomes to distinguish actively translated sequences from non-productive ribosomal binding.
source: Instead of profiling all ribosomal-bound mRNAs, we perform ribosome footprinting on polysomal fractions. In this way, mRNAs bound by multiple ribosomes and hence actively translated can be isolated and distinguished from mRNAs bound by sporadic, putatively non-productive single ribosomes or ribosomal subunits.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological approach developed in this study, supported by the experimental design.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq detected 191 annotated smORFs as translated in the initial small polysome experiment.
source: Altogether 191 annotated smORFs passed the cut-off values to be deemed translated in this initial Poly-Ribo-Seq experiment. This is ∼70% of the smORFs transcribed in S2 cells in the total mRNA controls (Figure 2D, small polysomes).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Poly-Ribo-Seq analysis with specific cut-off criteria applied.

claim: Extensive small polysome profiling detected translation of 224 smORFs.
source: This extensive small polysome profiling yielded nearly four times the number ORF-mapping reads obtained in the previous small polysome profiling (Supplementary file 1A) and detected translation of 224 smORFs (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data from the extensive experiment as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Combining three independent experiments provides evidence that 228 smORFs are translated out of 274 transcribed in S2 cells (83%).
source: By combining the three experiments, we provide evidence that 228 smORFs are translated out of 274 transcribed in S2 cells (83%), which is very similar to the proportion of standard length protein-coding ORFs translated (81%) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined data from three independent Poly-Ribo-Seq experiments.

claim: The proportion of annotated smORFs translated (83%) is similar to that of standard protein-coding ORFs (81%).
source: By combining the three experiments, we provide evidence that 228 smORFs are translated out of 274 transcribed in S2 cells (83%), which is very similar to the proportion of standard length protein-coding ORFs translated (81%) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim compares translation proportions between smORFs and standard ORFs based on experimental data.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq almost doubles the previous repertoire of translated smORFs in Drosophila from 164 to 285.
source: Altogether this data almost doubles the previous repertoire of translated smORFs in Drosophila from 164 to 285 (164 previously corroborated [Figure 1A] and 121 new translated smORFs).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing previous corroborated smORFs with newly detected ones from this study.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq detects 86% of smORFs with Peptide Atlas evidence in S2 cells (51 out of 59 smORFs).
source: Poly-Ribo-Seq detects 86% of smORFs with Peptide Atlas evidence in S2 cells (51 out of 59 smORFs; Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Poly-Ribo-Seq results with existing proteomic data from Peptide Atlas.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq detected 90 of the 99 smORFs in the combined proteomics pool.
source: Poly-Ribo-Seq revealed 228 smORFs as translated, including 90 of the 99 in the combined proteomics pool (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Poly-Ribo-Seq with combined proteomic data.

claim: All 12 smORFs tested by FLAG-tagging transfection assay were confirmed to be translated.
source: Transfection and staining of S2 cells with these FLAG-tagged smORFs confirmed the translation of all 12 smORFs tested, which exhibit a range of translational indicators (Figure 3A,B; Table 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation using FLAG-tagging and immunofluorescence.

claim: Six smORFs display a reticular distribution resembling mitochondria and co-localize with the mitochondrial marker Mitotracker Red.
source: Six smORFs display a reticular distribution resembling mitochondria, an inference supported by their co-localization with the mitochondrial marker Mitotracker Red (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E; Table 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data showing co-localization with mitochondrial markers.

claim: Six smORFs exhibited other types of anisotropic cytoplasmic localisation, indicating they may localise to other cytoplasmic compartments.
source: Six smORFs exhibited other types of anisotropic cytoplasmic localisation, similarly to ER-expressed Sarcolamban smORF (Magny et al., 2013), indicating that they may localise to other cytoplasmic compartments (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E; Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and comparison with known ER-localized smORF.

claim: 313 smORFs in non-coding RNA transcripts appear translated by Poly-Ribo-Seq.
source: 313 smORFs in these transcripts appear translated by Poly-Ribo-Seq (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by Poly-Ribo-Seq experimental data on non-coding RNAs.

claim: The median translation efficiency of smORFs within ncRNA genes is lower than for canonical genes and annotated smORFs, and is similar to UTRs.
source: The median translation efficiency of these putative smORFs within ncRNA genes is lower than for canonical genes and annotated smORFs, and in fact is similar to UTRs (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of translation efficiency metrics shown in Table 2.

claim: 2708 uORFs (30% of transcribed uORFs) are footprinted by ribosomes.
source: 9069 of these uORFs were transcribed in S2 cells and of these 2708 (30%) are footprinted by ribosomes (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Poly-Ribo-Seq data on upstream ORFs.

claim: Translated uORFs display lower median TE than canonical ORFs and translated smORFs.
source: Similarly to smORFs in putative non-coding RNAs, translated uORFs display lower median TE than canonical ORFs and translated smORFs (Table 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of translation efficiency values in Table 2.

claim: 93% of S2-translated smORFs have phastCons scores above 0.55, indicating conservation level similar to canonical long-ORFs.
source: 93% of S2-translated smORFs have phastCons scores above this threshold (median = 0.66), indicating a conservation level similar to that of canonical long-ORFs, and hence, a similar level of functionality for the coding sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of conservation scores across 12 insect species.

claim: Annotated smORFs display a lower than random usage of arginine, which is a hallmark of translated proteins.
source: Annotated smORFs display a lower than random usage of arginine, which is a hallmark of translated proteins (King and Jukes, 1969).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid composition analysis and comparison with established knowledge about translated proteins.

claim: Annotated smORFs display differential usage of several amino acids characteristic of alpha-helices, being enriched for lysine and phenylalanine, and depleted of serine.
source: However, they also display differential usage of several amino acids, which are characteristic of alpha-helices in canonical proteins, being enriched for lysine and phenylalanine, and depleted of serine (Chou and Fasman, 1974; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by amino acid composition analysis and comparison with known alpha-helix characteristics.

claim: About a third of translated smORFs contain putative transmembrane alpha-helix motifs.
source: This finding was corroborated by an abundance of putative transmembrane alpha-helix motifs, in about a third of translated smORFs (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic prediction using TMHMM software.

claim: About a third of all predicted smORFs contain putative transmembrane alpha-helix motifs, compared to the expected 20% observed in canonical proteins.
source: This finding was corroborated by an abundance of putative transmembrane alpha-helix motifs, in about a third of translated smORFs (Figure 4C) and all predicted smORFs (Figure 4D) compared to the expected 20% observed in canonical proteins (Krogh et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis and comparison with known proportions in canonical proteins.

claim: Over half of the translated smORFs have revealed a function in high-throughput S2 cell RNAi screens.
source: The putative functionality of smORF peptides is further supported by over half of the translated smORFs having revealed a function in high-throughput S2 cell RNAi screens in previous studies (Schmidt et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from previous RNAi screening studies.

claim: 196 of the translated smORFs are transcribed in embryos.
source: The biological relevance of smORFs is also implied by the transcription of 196 of these translated smORFs in embryos (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data from embryonic stages.

claim: 88 translated smORFs are transcribed throughout the whole of embryogenesis, which might be indicative of a basic cellular or housekeeping role.
source: 88 of these smORFs are transcribed throughout the whole of embryogenesis, which might be indicative of a basic cellular or housekeeping role
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data and inference about potential function based on expression pattern.

claim: 47 translated smORFs have stage-specific expression, perhaps indicative of a developmental role.
source: whereas 47 have stage-specific expression, perhaps indicative of a developmental role.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data and speculation about potential developmental function.

claim: The 555 annotated smORFs not transcribed in S2 cells share the bioinformatic characteristics of the smORFs detected as translated by Poly-Ribo-Seq.
source: The 555 annotated smORFs not transcribed in S2 cells, including 505 smORFs with uncorroborated translation, share the bioinformatic characteristics of the smORFs detected as translated by Poly-Ribo-Seq including: average peptide length (Figure 4E–F); amino acid usage (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A); and abundance of putative transmembrane alpha-helices (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic comparison of multiple characteristics between translated and non-transcribed smORFs.

claim: Results showing translation and possible peptide function for 83% of the smORFs transcribed in S2 cells could be extrapolated to the wider pool, potentially bringing the number of smORFs encoding functional peptides in Drosophila to around 700.
source: Therefore, our results showing translation and possible peptide function for 83% of the smORFs transcribed in S2 cells could be extrapolated to this wider pool, potentially bringing the number of smORFs encoding functional peptides in Drosophila to around 700.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation from experimental results to the broader set of annotated smORFs.

claim: No bioinformatic indicator (phastCons, size, aa composition) was able to distinguish translated uORFs and ncRNAs from intergenic or random sequences.
source: No indicator (phastCons, size, aa composition) was able to distinguish translated uORFs and ncRNAs from intergenic or random sequences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis comparing multiple characteristics.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq detects translation of two types of smORF: 'longer' smORFs producing peptides ~80 aa with bioinformatic hallmarks of peptide function, and 'dwarf' smORFs from ncRNAs and 5′-UTRs that are shorter (~20 aa), less efficiently translated, and missing such markers.
source: It appears that Poly-Ribo-Seq detects translation of two types of smORF: (a) 'longer' smORFs that are efficiently translated producing peptides ∼80 aa possessing bioinformatic hallmarks of peptide function; and (b) 'dwarf' smORFs translated from ncRNAs and 5′-UTRs, which are in general shorter (∼20 aa), less efficiently translated, and missing such bioinformatic and molecular markers.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive analysis of multiple characteristics distinguishing two classes of smORFs.

claim: Small polysomes contain mRNAs encoding long ORFs, but these have lower TE than when isolated from large polysomes.
source: Small polysomes contain mRNAs encoding long ORFs, but these have lower TE than when isolated from large polysomes (Table 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of translation efficiency values between small and large polysome fractions.

claim: The TE of smORFs from small polysomes is similar to the TE of long ORFs from large polysomes.
source: However, the TE of smORFs from small polysomes is similar to the TE of long ORFs from large polysomes, indicating that smORFs can be translated at similar levels to standard protein-coding ORFs (Table 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of translation efficiency values between different ORF types and polysome fractions.

claim: The genome-wide distribution of ribosome densities in two independent Poly-Ribo-Seq experiments was strongly correlated (R2 = 0.83).
source: The genome-wide distribution of ribosome densities in two independent Poly-Ribo-Seq experiments was strongly correlated (R2 = 0.83), suggesting that Poly-Ribo-Seq is highly reproducible (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis of two biological replicates.

claim: 80% of putative translated smORFs were detected in all three Poly-Ribo-Seq data sets.
source: The results of the three independent experiments are highly overlapping as 80% of putative translated smORFs were detected in all three data sets (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of results across three independent experiments.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq increases nearly fourfold the number of smORFs with evidence of translation in S2 cells from 59 (Peptide Atlas) to 228.
source: Poly-Ribo-Seq increases nearly fourfold the number of smORFs with evidence of translation in S2 cells from 59 (Peptide Atlas) to 228 (Poly-Ribo-Seq).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Poly-Ribo-Seq results with existing proteomic data.

claim: The Poly-Ribo-Seq RPKM values of smORFs detected by peptidomics are over three times as high as those that are not.
source: The Poly-Ribo-Seq RPKM values of smORFs detected by peptidomics are over three times as high as those that are not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mass spectrometry detects peptides arising from the most highly translated smORFs, as also observed by other authors (Brunner et al., 2007; Bazzini et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RPKM values and corroborated by citations to similar findings.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed the expected sizes of the tagged peptides.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed the expected sizes of the tagged peptides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot experimental data.

claim: The comparison of ribosomal footprinting reads with reads from polysomal fractions before footprinting shows a high correlation for canonical coding sequences but not for non-coding RNAs.
source: The comparison of ribosomal footprinting reads with reads resulting from the sequencing of RNA from polysomal fractions before footprinting (as in polysomal profiling) shows a high correlation for canonical coding sequences as expected (Smith et al., 2014), but not for non-coding RNAs, where high RNASeq polysomal counts do not necessarily result in significant footprinting (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of two types of sequencing data and citation to similar methodology.

claim: Positive-testing smORFs from non-coding RNAs show codon read-phasing.
source: Further, these positive-testing smORFs from non-coding RNAs show codon read-phasing (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ribosome footprint read distribution showing triplet periodicity.

claim: The median TE of all annotated protein-coding transcripts was significantly higher in CDSs compared to 5′- and 3′-UTRs.
source: We observed that the median TE of all annotated protein-coding transcripts was significantly higher in CDSs compared to 5′- and 3′-UTRs (Figure 1D) indicating that 'Poly-Ribo-Seq' defines regions of active translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of translation efficiency across different transcript regions.

claim: Triplet phasing is observed in the mapping of Poly-Ribo-Seq reads in coding sequences.
source: As previously reported for ribosomal profiling, we observe triplet phasing in the mapping of our Poly-Ribo-Seq reads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), reflecting the positioning of ribosomes on codons
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of read distribution patterns and comparison with previous ribosome profiling studies.

claim: Triplet phasing is not globally seen in UTRs.
source: which is not globally seen in UTRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of read distribution patterns in UTR regions.

claim: ∼80% of Poly-Ribo-Seq reads mapped to coding sequences of canonical protein-coding genes.
source: Our 'Poly-Ribo-Seq' captured regions of active translation as ∼80% of reads mapped to coding sequences of canonical protein-coding genes (Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by alignment statistics from sequencing data.

claim: Read densities drop off before the start and after stop codons in canonical protein-coding genes.
source: with read densities dropping off before the start and after stop codons (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by visualization of read density profiles across transcript features.

claim: Drosophila smORFs can be bound by up to six ribosomes.
source: Although RT-PCR of polysome sucrose gradient fractions confirmed that smORF mRNAs were enriched in small polysomes compared to large polysomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), it suggested that Drosophila smORFs can be bound by up to six ribosomes, perhaps reflecting a tighter packing of ribosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis of polysome fractions and inference about ribosome density.

claim: Small and large polysomes showed a marked difference in genome-wide ribosomal densities.
source: Small and large polysomes showed a marked difference in genome-wide ribosomal densities (Figure 2A), suggesting that these two fractions contain mRNAs translated at different levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of ribosome density distributions between polysome fractions.

claim: Small polysomes contained double the number of smORFs detected in large polysomes, and all smORFs detected in large polysomes were also present in small polysomes.
source: As intended, Poly-Ribo-Seq detected smORFs with translation signatures, and these were enriched in small polysomes, which contained double the number and all of the smORFs detected in large polysomes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of smORF detection between polysome fractions.

claim: The low smORF TE values in large polysomes are consistent with low levels of smORF mRNAs being present in large polysomal complexes.
source: The low smORF TE values in large polysomes are similarly consistent with low levels of smORF mRNAs being present in large polysomal complexes.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of translation efficiency data in the context of polysome composition.

claim: The annotation of the Drosophila genome contains double the proportion of predicted smORF-encoding genes than other metazoan genomes.
source: The annotation of the Drosophila genome contains double the proportion of predicted smORF-encoding genes than other metazoan genomes (some 829 smORF genes, or 4% of the total, Table 1) (FlyBase, Ensembl).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of smORF proportions across species shown in Table 1.

claim: Less than a quarter of annotated Drosophila smORFs have well-corroborated translation and peptide function.
source: However, closer scrutiny reveals that although these genes have well-corroborated transcriptional data (modENCODE), less than a quarter of these have corroborated translation and peptide function.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of available evidence for annotated smORFs from multiple sources.

claim: The 'corroborated' smORFs have in most cases a gene name and associated literature.
source: These 'corroborated' smORFs have in most cases a gene name (e.g., Defensin) and associated literature.
evidence: The claim is based on examination of annotation characteristics of corroborated smORFs.

claim: The majority of uncorroborated smORFs (494 smORFs) have no evidence of translation recorded.
source: The translation of the remaining 665 putative smORFs is thus not yet fully proven, and in most cases (494 smORFs) no evidence of translation is recorded.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of available evidence for annotated smORFs.

claim: Most uncorroborated smORFs only have a cognate identifier and their 'coding' status varies between genome releases.
source: The majority of these 'uncorroborated' smORFs only have a cognate identifier (e.g., CG34200) and their 'coding' status varies between genome releases (unpublished observation).
evidence: The claim is based on examination of annotation characteristics and unpublished observations.

claim: Ribosome profiling has corroborated and expanded the proteomes of yeast, mouse, zebrafish, and Drosophila.
source: The new technique of ribosome profiling has corroborated and expanded the proteomes of yeast (Ingolia et al., 2009; Duncan and Mata, 2014; Smith et al., 2014), mouse (Ingolia et al., 2011), zebrafish (Chew et al., 2013; Bazzini et al., 2014), and Drosophila (Dunn et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple ribosome profiling studies across different organisms.

claim: Thousands of new translated sequences have been described by ribosome profiling in each species studied.
source: Thousands of new translated sequences have been described in each case, whether novel exons of annotated genes, alternative initiation sites, or entire ORFs.
evidence: The claim is based on summary of findings from multiple cited ribosome profiling studies.

claim: A ribosomal footprint cannot always be equated with translation; non-productive binding of single ribosomes to mRNAs and scanning 40S ribosomal subunits can result in footprints.
source: The problem remains that a ribosomal footprint cannot always be equated with translation; non-productive binding of single ribosomes to mRNAs and scanning 40S ribosomal subunits can result in footprints, yet do not constitute translation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about limitations of ribosome profiling methodology.

claim: It has been suggested that some smORFs associate with ribosomes in a non-productive manner and do not undergo productive translation.
source: It has been suggested that some smORFs associate with ribosomes in such a non-productive manner and do not undergo productive translation (Wilson and Masel, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to a previous study suggesting non-productive ribosome association.

claim: smORF mRNAs are short and present a small target for ribosomal binding and generation of footprints, potentially making traditional ribosome profiling less suitable for the study of smORFs.
source: Moreover, smORF mRNAs are short and present a small target for ribosomal binding and generation of footprints, potentially making traditional ribosome profiling less suitable for the study of smORFs.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of ribosome profiling for short sequences.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq may overlook very short smORFs that cannot fit multiple ribosomes, but this loss should be offset by the increased stringency of discarding false positive footprints.
source: Although this method may overlook very short smORFs that cannot fit multiple ribosomes, this loss should be offset by the increased stringency of discarding false positive footprints.
evidence: The claim is based on logical reasoning about the trade-offs of the Poly-Ribo-Seq methodology.

claim: Extrapolation of results suggests that thousands of smORFs are translated in higher organisms.
source: Extrapolation of our results suggests that thousands of smORFs are translated in higher organisms and that smORFs could have diverse functions, including expression of peptides active in cell membranes.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation from Drosophila results to other organisms.

claim: smORFs could have diverse functions, including expression of peptides active in cell membranes.
source: Extrapolation of our results suggests that thousands of smORFs are translated in higher organisms and that smORFs could have diverse functions, including expression of peptides active in cell membranes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from bioinformatic analysis and localization data.

claim: Targeted bioinformatic approaches predict that hundreds of smORFs could be translated and functional in bacteria, yeast, plants and metazoans.
source: Targeted bioinformatic approaches predict that hundreds of smORFs could be translated and functional in bacteria (Hemm et al., 2008), yeast (Basrai et al., 1997; Kastenmayer et al., 2006), plants (Hanada et al., 2012) and metazoans including Drosophila (Ladoukakis et al., 2011), mouse (Frith et al., 2006; Crappe et al., 2013), and humans (Slavoff et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple bioinformatic prediction studies across different organisms.

claim: The predicted number of translated smORFs is in contrast to their low rate of detection in biochemical (proteomic) and functional (genetic) screens.
source: but this is in contrast to their low rate of detection in biochemical (proteomic) (Falth et al., 2006; Slavoff et al., 2013) and functional (genetic) (Kumar et al., 2002) screens.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to proteomic and genetic screening studies.

claim: The annotation of smORFs has been hindered by their size: short sequences are unable to obtain the high conservation scores that are the accepted indicator of functionality.
source: Small open reading frames (smORFs) of fewer than 100 amino acids exist in eukaryotic genomes in hundreds of thousands, but their annotation has been hindered by their size: short sequences are unable to obtain the high conservation scores that are the accepted indicator of functionality (Ladoukakis et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about annotation challenges and citation to relevant study.

claim: Limited numbers of experimentally proven functional smORFs exist in eukaryotes.
source: This handicap, coupled with the limited numbers of experimentally proven functional smORFs in eukaryotes (Kastenmayer et al., 2006; Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007; Hanada et al., 2012; Magny et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014; reviewed in Andrews and Rothnagel, 2014), has so far precluded the reliable annotation of smORFs as coding sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies of functional smORFs and a review.

claim: The limited number of experimentally proven functional smORFs has precluded the reliable annotation of smORFs as coding sequences.
source: This handicap, coupled with the limited numbers of experimentally proven functional smORFs in eukaryotes (Kastenmayer et al., 2006; Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007; Hanada et al., 2012; Magny et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014; reviewed in Andrews and Rothnagel, 2014), has so far precluded the reliable annotation of smORFs as coding sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the state of smORF annotation given the limited experimental evidence.

claim: The translation of 190 smORFs has been detected in zebrafish.
source: Consistent with this prediction the translation of 190 smORFs has been detected in one such experiment in zebrafish (Bazzini et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a zebrafish ribosome profiling study.

claim: Extrapolation of results in flies and zebrafish strongly suggests that hundreds of smORFs are translated in higher organisms, including in humans and other mammals.
source: Extrapolation of these two sets of results in flies and zebrafish strongly suggests that hundreds of smORFs are translated in higher organisms, including in humans and other mammals.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation from experimental results in two model organisms to other species.

claim: Experimental evidence and full functional characterisation is the only way to ascertain the translation and function of each individual smORF.
source: While bioinformatics can be useful in unearthing smORF candidates, ultimately experimental evidence and full functional characterisation is the only way to ascertain the translation and function of each individual smORF.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about the limitations of bioinformatics and the need for experimental validation.

claim: The human genome contains some 32,000 transcripts currently annotated as long non-coding RNAs.
source: The human genome contains some 32,000 transcripts currently annotated as long non-coding RNAs (Volders et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a database or study of long non-coding RNAs.

claim: Around 44% of long-non-coding RNAs have been detected in the cytoplasm.
source: and a fraction around 44% of long-non-coding RNAs have been detected in the cytoplasm (Derrien et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study of lncRNA subcellular localization.

claim: If cytoplasmic lncRNAs were translated in the same proportion as found in Drosophila (34%), there could be thousands of human peptides awaiting detection and characterisation.
source: If these cytoplasmic lncRNAs were corroborated and translated in the same proportion as we find here in Drosophila (some 34%), there could be thousands of human peptides awaiting detection and characterisation.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation from Drosophila results to human genome.

claim: The small size of both uORF and ncORF peptides may hinder their detection by mass spectrometry.
source: The small size of both uORF and ncORF peptides may hinder their detection by mass spectrometry, as in the case of peptides translated by the Drosophila genes tal and scl (unpublished observation)
evidence: The claim is based on inference about technical limitations of mass spectrometry and unpublished observations.

claim: Absence of proteomic detection or functional data should not be used to disprove translation of uORFs and ncORFs.
source: and so absence of proteomic detection (or absence of functional data, see below) should not be used to disprove their translation.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about the limitations of proteomic and functional methods for small peptides.

claim: Poly-Ribo-Seq can define the whole of the translated ORF as opposed to isolated micropeptides detected by peptidomics.
source: Furthermore, Poly-Ribo-Seq can define the whole of the translated ORF as opposed to isolated micropeptides detected by peptidomics.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the capabilities of Poly-Ribo-Seq versus peptidomics.

claim: High peptide translation level seems a critical factor (but likely not the only one) favouring detection by mass spectrometry.
source: High peptide translation level seems a critical factor (but likely not the only one) favouring detection by mass spectrometry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that highly translated smORFs are more likely to be detected by proteomics.

claim: The combination of Poly-Ribo-Seq and peptidomics could produce interesting data on peptide stability and degradation.
source: However, the combination of Poly-Ribo-Seq and peptidomics could produce interesting data on peptide stability and degradation.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential future applications of combining methods.

claim: Most annotated and translated smORFs have conservation levels similar to canonical proteins.
source: We observe that most annotated and translated smORFs have conservation levels similar to canonical proteins and have so far displayed functionality in RNAi tests in some 50% of the cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation analysis and RNAi screening data.

claim: Translated smORFs have displayed functionality in RNAi tests in some 50% of the cases.
source: We observe that most annotated and translated smORFs have conservation levels similar to canonical proteins and have so far displayed functionality in RNAi tests in some 50% of the cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from RNAi screening experiments.

claim: Translated smORFs encode peptides of around 80 aa with a high proportion of transmembrane alpha-helix motifs.
source: They encode peptides of around 80 aa with a high proportion of transmembrane alpha-helix motifs, in agreement with their overall pattern of amino acid composition.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of peptide length and structural motifs.

claim: The bioinformatic indicators of translated smORFs appear similar in the 505 uncorroborated smORFs not transcribed in S2 cells.
source: Their bioinformatic indicators (conservation, size, aa usage, and transmembrane motifs) appear similar in the 505 uncorroborated smORFs not transcribed in S2 cells, suggesting that, if translated, some 700 smORFs might encode peptides with similar functional potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic comparison and leads to speculation about functional potential.

claim: Corroborated smORFs display a variety of functions as antibacterial peptides, cell signals, cytoskeletal regulators, and other regulators of canonical proteins.
source: The corroborated smORFs display a variety of functions as antibacterial peptides (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007), cell signals (Pueyo and Couso, 2008), cytoskeletal regulators (Djakovic et al., 2006), and other regulators of canonical proteins (Hanyu-Nakamura et al., 2008; Magny et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple functional studies of specific smORFs.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis shows that the most abundant terms amongst previously corroborated smORFs are ribosome constituents, oxidoreductase activity, and transporter activity.
source: GO term enrichment analysis shows that the most abundant terms amongst previously corroborated smORFs are ribosome constituents, oxidoreductase activity, and transporter activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Amongst uncorroborated smORFs, the frequency of predicted transmembrane alpha-helix motifs is the highest.
source: The last two imply an association with biological membranes, and it is thus interesting that amongst uncorroborated smORFs, the frequency of predicted transmembrane alpha-helix motifs is the highest.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of transmembrane motif predictions.

claim: Hundreds of small, membrane-associated peptides are awaiting characterisation.
source: We surmise that hundreds of small, membrane-associated peptides are awaiting characterisation, and they may alter our understanding of many cellular and organismal processes of biological and medical relevance.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on extrapolation from bioinformatic and localization data.

claim: Small membrane-associated peptides may alter our understanding of many cellular and organismal processes of biological and medical relevance.
source: We surmise that hundreds of small, membrane-associated peptides are awaiting characterisation, and they may alter our understanding of many cellular and organismal processes of biological and medical relevance.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the potential impact of discovering new smORF functions.

claim: Small peptides would interact with canonical proteins as their regulators, as their size limits their structural capabilities.
source: We expect that these peptides would interact with canonical proteins as their regulators (Magny et al., 2013), as their size limits their structural capabilities; though, such capabilities could be expanded by oligomerization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about peptide function given size constraints, supported by citation to a regulatory example.

claim: The structural capabilities of small peptides could be expanded by oligomerization.
source: We expect that these peptides would interact with canonical proteins as their regulators (Magny et al., 2013), as their size limits their structural capabilities; though, such capabilities could be expanded by oligomerization.
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential mechanisms for small peptide function.

claim: The main described function of most uORFs is to regulate translation of downstream long ORFs.
source: The main described function of most uORFs is to regulate translation of downstream long ORFs, either interfering with the translation of the downstream ORF, or collecting ribosomes in order to promote it.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about uORF function from the literature.

claim: The translated uORF peptide (and hence its aa sequence) can be irrelevant for its regulatory function.
source: The translated uORF peptide (and hence its aa sequence) can be irrelevant ([Child et al., 1999; Kulkarni et al., 2011] reviewed in Kozak, 2005; Andrews and Rothnagel, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing peptide-independent uORF function.

claim: A cis-regulatory role for uORFs would fit with the low TE and the high sequence variability (low phastCons scores) observed for uORFs.
source: Such a cis-regulatory role would fit with the low TE and the high sequence variability (low phastCons scores) observed for uORFs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference connecting observed data patterns with known regulatory mechanisms.

claim: There is no overall positive or negative correlation between the translation of uORFs and that of their main downstream ORF.
source: However, we do not observe an overall positive or negative correlation between the translation of uORFs and that of their main downstream ORF (unpublished observation)
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished analysis of the relationship between uORF and downstream ORF translation.

claim: Validating uORF function is difficult, since much of the current functional data is based on conditions that knock-out whole transcripts.
source: Validating uORF function is difficult, since much of the current functional (genetics) data is based on conditions (gene deficiencies, promotor mutations, RNAi) that knock-out whole transcripts, that is, both the short uORF peptide and the downstream long-canonical protein.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about the limitations of genetic methods for studying uORFs.

claim: The smORFs in putative long non-coding RNAs with ribosomal signatures might reveal either coding potential, a non-coding association with ribosomes, or a dual function as coding and non-coding for these transcripts.
source: The smORFs in putative long non-coding RNAs with ribosomal signatures might reveal either coding potential, a non-coding association with ribosomes, or a dual function as coding and non-coding for these transcripts.
evidence: The claim is speculative about possible interpretations of ribosome association with lncRNAs.

claim: Standard genetic techniques are unable to distinguish between coding and non-coding functions of lncRNAs.
source: Again, standard genetic techniques are unable to distinguish between these possibilities.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about the limitations of genetic methods.

claim: The genes tal and scl were previously annotated as putative non-coding RNAs but encode functional peptides.
source: This group of smORFs has the potential to encode functional peptides, as shown by the genes tal and scl, that were previously annotated as putative non-coding RNAs. These genes encode peptides as short as 11 and 28 aa with important functions in development and physiology (Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007; Magny et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to functional studies of tal and scl.

claim: tal and scl encode peptides as short as 11 and 28 aa with important functions in development and physiology.
source: These genes encode peptides as short as 11 and 28 aa with important functions in development and physiology (Galindo et al., 2007; Kondo et al., 2007; Magny et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: In the case of Scl, a transmembrane alpha-helical structure was corroborated.
source: In the case of Scl, a transmembrane alpha-helical structure was corroborated (Magny et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a structural study of Scl.

claim: A manual study of tal and scl homologies identified their conservation in distant species.
source: Further, a manual study of their homologies identified their conservation in distant species.
evidence: The claim is based on manual bioinformatic analysis of sequence conservation.

claim: A case-by-case bioinformatic and experimental examination of ncRNA smORFs may reveal unknown numbers of new bioactive peptides.
source: Thus, a case-by-case bioinformatic and experimental examination of ncRNA smORFs may reveal unknown numbers of new bioactive peptides.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the potential for discovering new functional peptides.

claim: Thousands of smORFs are translated in metazoan genomes.
source: Altogether our data indicate that thousands of smORFs are translated in metazoan genomes.
evidence: The claim is based on extrapolation from experimental data in Drosophila to other metazoans.

claim: There exist two broad types of translated smORFs: 'longer' smORFs and 'dwarf' smORFs.
source: However, they also suggest the existence of two broad types of translated smORFs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence distinguishing two smORF classes.

claim: 'Longer' smORFs produce conserved 80 aa-long peptides whose translation efficiencies resemble those of canonical proteins and with functions biased towards an association with cell membranes.
source: The 'longer' smORFs produce conserved 80 aa-long peptides whose translation efficiencies resemble those of canonical proteins and with functions biased towards an association with cell membranes.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple types of data including conservation, translation efficiency, and functional predictions.

claim: 'Dwarf' smORFs are mostly found in 5′-UTRs and non-coding RNAs, are not detected by gene prediction programs, and on average encode peptides of some 20 aa-long.
source: The 'dwarf' smORFs are mostly found in 5′-UTRs and non-coding RNAs, are not detected by gene prediction programs, and on average encode peptides of some 20 aa-long.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of smORF locations, sizes, and detection by prediction tools.

claim: 'Dwarf' smORFs are less conserved, translated at lower efficiencies, and of unclear function.
source: They are also less conserved, translated at lower efficiencies, and of unclear function as yet.
evidence: The claim is based on conservation analysis, translation efficiency measurements, and lack of functional indicators.
